Study Abstract

Background. Electronic health record (EHR) data from community-based naturopathic clinics are a largely underutilized resource for health services research. Prior studies of naturopathic practice have relied on billing and administrative data, which fail to document the lifestyle counseling, supplement recommendations, and clinical reasoning that are central to naturopathic care.

Objectives. To develop and validate a privacy-first, cloud-based informatics pipeline to extract, de-identify, and structure both clinical records and free-text notes from multi-clinic naturopathic EHRs, and to demonstrate the utility of the resulting research database through population-level practice characterization and glycemic cohort analysis.

Methods. EHR data were extracted via FHIR API from seven ChARM-based naturopathic clinics in Washington State and stored in Google Cloud Platform under a HIPAA-compliant Business Associate Agreement. De-identification was performed using the Google Cloud Healthcare API and a manually audited custom redaction pipeline. De-identified clinical notes (n=858,394) were parsed into 12 naturopathic treatment categories; manual review of a random sample confirmed 97.9% of extracted treatments were correctly classified. Two glycemic cohorts were defined: longitudinal (≥2 HbA1c readings; n=5,576) and treatment pattern (HbA1c ≥5.7% with ≥1 treatment order; n=2,965). Linear regression examined the association between hs-CRP and HbA1c (n=4,371).

Results. The database includes 58,498 patients, 469,162 encounters, 858,394 clinical notes, and 3.6 million observations across 7 clinics (2008–2026); 68.1% female, mean age 42.7 years. Analytic utility was confirmed: longitudinal HbA1c analysis documented significant reductions over time in the prediabetes (−0.131%; p<0.001) and diabetes (−0.766%; p<0.001) subgroups; treatment pattern analysis identified supplements, diet, and exercise as a frequently co-prescribed triad; and linear regression confirmed a significant positive association between hs-CRP and HbA1c, consistent with published literature.

Conclusions. This methods-feasibility pilot demonstrates that a HIPAA-compliant cloud pipeline can transform heterogeneous, multi-clinic naturopathic EHR data into a validated research dataset, establishing proof of concept for a platform designed for expansion to a broader, more representative sample of naturopathic practices.

HbA1c Cohort Analysis
Used to test analytic utility of the database
Cohorts used in this section:
  • Elevated HbA1c cohort (n=2,965): patients with any HbA1c ≥5.7% (prediabetes or diabetes range) and at least one documented treatment order. Used for treatment frequency, treatment co-occurrence, and diagnosis concordance analyses.
  • Longitudinal HbA1c cohort (n=1,582): patients with ≥2 HbA1c readings on distinct dates, first reading ≥5.7%. Used for glycemic change and LME analyses. Includes 1,582 elevated-baseline patients plus 3,994 normoglycemic patients as an internal comparator.
    • LME analysis: n=765 (further restricted to adults ≥18, valid birth sex, BMI available, ≥30-day reading gap)
Cohort definitions are canonical BigQuery views (cohort_elevated_hba1c, cohort_longitudinal_hba1c) sourced from standardized_observations, which captures both LOINC-coded and display-name-identified HbA1c records.

n = 12,735 patients; first HbA1c reading per patient; 0.2% bins; Catmull-Rom smoothed

ICD-10: E10.x = Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus; E11.x = Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; R73.x = Elevated blood glucose / prediabetes. T1DM and T2DM counts are not mutually exclusive. “Prediabetes only” excludes patients with any T1/T2 code.

Longitudinal HbA1c: Change from First to Last Reading

  • Paired t-test, first vs. last HbA1c reading per patient

Treatment × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

What is a linear mixed effects model?
A linear mixed effects (LME) model is designed for data where the same individuals are measured repeatedly over time. Rather than treating each HbA1c reading as independent, it estimates a shared population-level trajectory while allowing each patient to start at their own personal baseline level (the “random intercept”). Treatment × time interaction terms then ask: do patients with documented receipt of a given treatment show a systematically faster or slower rate of HbA1c change compared to patients without that treatment, after adjusting for covariates? The coefficient β/yr is the additional annual HbA1c change associated with each treatment, relative to the reference slope.

Model & Cohort

Outcome: HbA1c at each visit. Fixed effects: time, baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication, clinic. Random intercept per patient. 12 treatment categories tested simultaneously (Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.0042). Cohort: n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; median follow-up 400 days; ICC = 0.28 (confirms within-patient clustering warrants mixed model). Reference slope (no treatment, no medication): -0.0941 %/yr.

Interpretation

  • Botanical Medicine (n=135; β = -0.0485 %/yr, p=0.007 **) showed nominally significant associations with faster HbA1c improvement. None survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.0042 for 12 simultaneous tests). All findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
  • Conventional diabetes medications (n=45) are included as a confounder control (β = -0.0471 %/yr, p=0.052). Medicated patients entered care with a higher mean baseline HbA1c (6.91% vs. 6.06%), so including this term prevents confounding of naturopathic treatment estimates.
  • Most treatment categories — including diet/nutrition, exercise, stress/mindfulness, sleep hygiene, supplements, acupuncture, and IV therapy — did not reach nominal significance. The null result for diet counseling likely reflects heterogeneity in recommendations and the gap between documented counseling and patient adherence, rather than an absence of dietary effects on glycemic control.

Diet Subtype × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

Same LME structure as the primary treatment analysis, but treatment flags are five collapsed diet subcategories derived from the subcategory field in the treatments table. Reference group: patients with no named diet subtype documented (n=37 after overlap). Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.01. All findings are exploratory.

Model & Cohort

n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; ICC = 0.29; median follow-up 400 days. Reference slope (no diet subtype, no medication): -0.0515 %/yr. Covariates: baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication × time, clinic fixed effects.

Results

▼ Diet subtype categories

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Amber row = medication (confounder). Sorted by β. Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.01.

Interpretation

  • No diet subtype survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.01 for 5 simultaneous tests). All findings should be treated as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
  • Low carb / Keto (n=37) showed the largest nominally significant effect: β = -0.0448 %/yr (p=0.054), but does not survive correction and the subgroup is small. The direction is consistent with the evidence base for low-carbohydrate diets and glycemic control.
  • Whole foods / Mediterranean (n=189) trended favorably (β = -0.0225 %/yr, p=0.203) with the largest subgroup of the named diet types, suggesting this is worth examining in a larger sample.
  • General dietary guidance (n=296) showed a mildly positive trend (β = +0.0453 %/yr, p=0.005), likely reflecting that generic counseling is documented in more complex patients where no specific diet pattern has been identified — a form of clinical refractoriness rather than a diet effect.
  • Intermittent fasting and Elimination / Anti-inflammatory were essentially null. These categories have sufficient sample sizes to detect moderate effects, suggesting they are either genuinely ineffective in this cohort or that adherence to documented recommendations is too variable to detect a signal.

Botanical Subcategory × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

Same LME structure as the primary treatment analysis above, but the Herbs & Botanicals category is split into five individual agents: berberine, curcumin/turmeric, ashwagandha, rhodiola, and adaptogen (a broad category for herbal adaptogens not individually specified by name in clinical notes — e.g., eleuthero, schisandra, holy basil). All other treatment categories are retained as fixed-effect covariates. Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.0100.

Model & Cohort

n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; ICC = 0.29. Reference slope (no treatment, no medication): -0.0823 %/yr. Covariates: baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication × time, clinic fixed effects, and all other treatment categories.

Botanical n β/yr 95% CI p-value
Curcumin / Turmeric 40 -0.0922 [-0.1434, -0.0410] <0.001 ***

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Negative β = faster HbA1c decline (improvement). Sorted by β.

Interpretation

  • Curcumin / Turmeric (n=40) showed the strongest individual botanical association with HbA1c improvement: β = -0.0922 %/yr (95% CI [-0.1434, -0.0410], p=<0.001). This is the only agent to survive Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.0100 for 5 tests). This signal is consistent with existing trial evidence for curcumin and metabolic markers, and likely drives the aggregate Herbs & Botanicals signal in the primary LME above. The subgroup (n=40) is modest; this is hypothesis-generating.
  • Berberine (n=124) showed a negative trend (β = -0.0311 %/yr, p=0.064) but did not reach nominal significance after adjusting for other botanical agents. Berberine has established glucose-lowering properties (comparable to metformin in some trials); the modest effect size likely reflects co-prescription with other agents in this population, attenuating its independent signal.
  • Adaptogen showed nominally significant positive associations (slower improvement). As with other treatment-refractoriness signals in this dataset, these likely reflect more complex or treatment-resistant presentations rather than any causal effect of the agent.
  • All findings are exploratory and represent associations in an observational, non-randomized dataset. Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.0100. The Adaptogen category captures herbal adaptogens documented by category name rather than individual herb — commonly eleuthero, schisandra, holy basil, and similar — and represents patients for whom the clinician's note specified adaptogen support without naming a specific botanical.

HbA1c – hs-CRP Regression Analysis

Elevated HbA1c and elevated hs-CRP frequently co-occur: chronic low-grade inflammation promotes insulin resistance, while hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling. This analysis tests whether that relationship holds in our naturopathic patient cohort and examines whether the association differs between females and males. hs-CRP levels are systematically higher in females due to estrogen-mediated upregulation of hepatic CRP synthesis, motivating a sex-stratified analysis. We report a pooled model (sex as covariate), an interaction model (log CRP × sex), and sex-stratified regressions. One observation per patient (first recorded value); adults ≥18 with all variables present (n=4,371: F=2,891, M=1,480).

Female2,891+0.0508<0.001 ***+0.0092+0.01160.106
Male1,480+0.05960.003 **+0.0111+0.01630.065

Interpretation. In the pooled model (adj. R² = 0.098), log(hs-CRP) was a significant independent predictor of HbA1c (β = +0.0530; p<0.001), with age (β = +0.0098; p<0.001), BMI (β = +0.0128; p<0.001), and male sex (β = +0.1346; p<0.001) also significant. The interaction term (log CRP × male sex) was not significant (β = +0.0213; p=0.224), indicating the slope of the CRP–HbA1c relationship does not differ meaningfully between sexes. Sex-stratified models confirm this: females show β = +0.0508 (adj. R² = 0.106) and males β = +0.0596 (adj. R² = 0.065), with both associations significant (p<0.001 and p=0.003, respectively). The lower adj. R² in males likely reflects the smaller male sample (n=1,480) and the narrower HbA1c range in this predominantly normoglycemic cohort. Overall, the CRP–HbA1c association is consistent with the published literature and similar in direction and magnitude across sexes.
